solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Nothing on record that identifies business

indicators.note: in an across clue, one thing placed 'on' another is written after it, as if leaning on it from the right

parts.note: a log is a written record, as a ship's log
nothing = O, the zero

explanation.surface: Someone scours the files for a document proving what a firm does, and finds nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a descriptive phrase standing for a noun: the thing that identifies a business.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by function: a company's emblem exists to make the firm recognisable at a glance.

clue.text: Made in desperate hurry, glass apt to shatter

indicators.note: glass that shatters breaks into pieces, and the pieces of GLASS APT are put back together in a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

explanation.surface: Something knocked together in a rush out of glass that is likely to break.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Glass apt to shatter' reads as a warning about fragile work; the fragility is the instruction to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: a last-gasp effort comes at the final moment, with the frantic haste of someone nearly out of breath.

clue.text: Conducted over good lab frequently

parts.note: conducted = guided, led round
O = over, the cricket abbreviation
G = good

explanation.surface: A report on a scientific laboratory that has repeatedly been run well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lab' looks like a laboratory, but it is short for Labrador, the breed most often trained to lead blind people.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example, reversed: Labradors are the usual breed for this work, so a lab frequently is one.

clue.text: Where one might find food writers of little talent?

definitions.meaning: grub is slang for food, so read literally this is a road full of it
a London street name that became shorthand for hack writers as a class

explanation.surface: A question about where to track down second-rate cookery writers.
explanation.walkthrough: Grub Street, in 18th-century London, was home to impoverished hack writers, and the name still stands for them. The clue also reads it literally, as a street of grub (food).
explanation.definitionFit: A literal reading (a street of grub) and a metonym: the address came to mean the hacks who lived there.

clue.text: Put down, then men raised mast on high

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising something lifts it so it reads from bottom to top

parts.note: to lay something is to put it down
OR = other ranks, soldiers who are not officers

explanation.surface: Someone sets something down, then a crew hoists a mast.
explanation.walkthrough: On a square-rigged ship the royal is the mast section (and sail) above the topgallant, the highest part of the rig.
explanation.definitionFit: A nautical term: the royal is the topmost section of a sailing ship's mast, so it is the mast on high.

clue.text: Iranian starts to throw boot about and waves ruler?

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter, so take the openings of 'throw' and 'boot'
letters thrown about are scattered and land in a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder
the first letters of Throw and Boot

explanation.surface: An Iranian hurls a boot around and waves at a monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Waves' looks like a verb of greeting; it is a noun, from the song Rule, Britannia!, whose heroine rules the waves.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic allusion: the song's refrain has her ruling the waves, so she is the waves' ruler, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Chief is after mean man who's paid pennies for position in front row

indicators.note: one thing coming after another in the answer, so the chief follows the mean one

parts.note: tight = stingy, mean with money
a chief is the head
a pro, a professional, is paid, unlike an amateur
p = pennies

explanation.surface: A boss follows a miserly employer who pays his staff a pittance, for a front-row seat.
explanation.walkthrough: The front row here is a rugby scrum, not a theatre: this player packs down on the right-hand side of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A sporting term: in rugby union the front row of the scrum is a hooker flanked by two props, loosehead and tighthead.

clue.text: Make one's mark in plea over a major departure from scripture

indicators.note: one thing placed in another sits inside it, so the mark-making goes inside the plea
in a down clue, turning something over flips it end to end, so it reads upwards

parts.note: to sue is to plead or petition
DO an X, the cross made by someone signing who cannot write

explanation.surface: Someone making an impression in court while appealing over a big break from religious teaching.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on both senses: a book of the Bible, and a mass departure, the Israelites leaving Egypt.
explanation.definitionFit: A double sense: the second book of the Old Testament narrates the Israelites' mass departure from Egypt.

clue.text: Band of fur in untidy place on cat, for one

indicators.note: in a down clue, one thing 'on' another rests on top of it, so it comes first

parts.note: a tip is a rubbish dump in Britain, so any messy place, as in 'your room is a tip'
a cat is one example of a pet

explanation.surface: A strip of fur left lying in a messy spot on the cat.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface puts the fur on the cat; in fact the untidy place goes on top of the cat's category.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain description: the garment is a narrow fur scarf or shoulder cape, a band of fur.

clue.text: Prison reformer's quick meal

parts.note: stir is slang for prison
Elizabeth Fry, the 19th-century English prison reformer

explanation.surface: A snack eaten by a campaigner for better jails.
explanation.walkthrough: Elizabeth Fry was a Quaker who campaigned to improve British prisons; she appeared on the old £5 note.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by quality: food tossed fast over high heat, ready in minutes.

clue.text: Richest countries unprepared in retrospect for conflict

parts.note: the developed, richest nations, as opposed to the Third World

indicators.note: retrospect is looking back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: raw = untrained, unprepared

explanation.surface: Wealthy nations, looking back, were not ready for fighting.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a fair historical claim about 1914, which is why the answer hides so well inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by category: the 1914–18 war is one specific conflict.

clue.text: Cliquey crowd pouring out

indicators.note: 'out' as in put out of place, so the letters leave their order

parts.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: An exclusive gang spilling out of a venue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pouring out' reads as one phrase about a crowd leaving; split it and 'out' is the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym: an exclusive circle that keeps others out is a clique.

clue.text: Lure a girl in a way that could be irregular

indicators.text: in a way that could be
indicators.note: the letters could be set out in another way, so they are rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

explanation.surface: Advice that chatting someone up might be an unconventional business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Irregular' looks like an adjective describing the seduction; it is a noun, an irregular soldier.
explanation.definitionFit: A military sense: irregulars are fighters outside the regular army, as partisan fighters are.

clue.text: Right about start of conflict and its end maybe

indicators.note: 'about' as in around, so one word goes round the letter

parts.note: right = true, correct

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of Conflict

explanation.surface: A comment on how a war begins and how it might finish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Its' points back to 'conflict', so the definition means the end of a conflict; 'maybe' admits not every one ends so.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a ceasefire agreement is one way a conflict can end.

clue.text: Cheats alter boring summer clothes

indicators.note: to bore is to drill into something, so one word goes inside another

parts.note: shorts are worn in summer
to alter is to change

explanation.surface: Swindlers adjust dull holiday outfits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boring' pretends to describe the clothes as dull; it is the drilling sense, and the answer is a verb matching 'Cheats'.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym by origin: giving a customer too little change was the original cheat, and it widened to any swindle.

clue.text: Rash, like hives or herpes for example

definitions.meaning: the adjective: impetuous, acting without thought

definitions.text: like hives or herpes for example
definitions.meaning: both words begin with H, and H stands for hot, as on a tap

explanation.surface: A list of skin rashes: hives, herpes and the like.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rash' looks like a skin complaint, backed up by hives and herpes, but the definition is the adjective. The second half is a joke: those words are H-headed, and H is hot.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym for impetuous, plus a jokey literal reading: words whose head (first letter) is H, for hot.

clue.text: Make fullest use of proverb first to explain gripping lives

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter
to grip is to hold, so the outer letters hold the inner ones

parts.note: a maxim is a proverb, a wise saying
the first letter of Explain
is = lives, exists

explanation.surface: Get the most out of a saying by using it to account for how people live.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gripping' looks like 'fascinating', but it is a container instruction; 'lives' is the verb, not the plural of life.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to get the most out of something is to make the fullest use of it.

clue.text: People on night train going over these?

definitions.text: People on night train going over these?

parts.note: passengers who doze in the berths overnight
the train runs over the beams the rails are laid on

explanation.surface: A riddle about passengers travelling overnight by rail.
explanation.walkthrough: The train passes over sleepers, the British name for railway ties, while more sleepers lie in its berths.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses of one word: dozing passengers, and the timber or concrete beams under the track.

clue.text: Pass on traffic warning and fix with utmost vigour

indicators.note: in an across clue, one thing placed 'on' another is written after it

parts.note: a toot of the horn warns other road users
to pass something is to hand it
to nail is to fix in place

explanation.surface: A driver passes on a warning about the traffic and then vigorously makes repairs.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer's AND is not the clue's 'and': the split falls inside the word, so the clue's 'and' merely joins.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: fighting as if with teeth and fingernails means using every ounce of strength.

clue.text: Initially simple lock creating tension

indicators.note: at the start, so take the word's first letter

parts.note: the first letter of Simple
a lock of hair is a tress

explanation.surface: A basic door lock causing anxiety.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lock' suggests a door, but it is a lock of hair.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, in both the physical sense (strain on a material) and the mental one.

clue.text: Flex performing as barrier

parts.note: a flex is the British word for an electrical cord
a performer is on, on stage

explanation.surface: Showing off one's muscles while acting as a blockade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flex' reads as a verb, flexing muscles; it is a noun, the cable on an appliance.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym: a line of police or tape set round an area bars people from it.

clue.text: Ugly dwarf in part of Austria, not unknown having doubled back

indicators.note: 'not unknown' means without the unknown, so that letter is taken away
the back of a word is its last letter, and doubling it writes that letter twice

parts.note: the Tyrol, an Alpine region of Austria
the last letter written a second time
Y, an algebraic unknown, is removed

explanation.surface: A hideous little man living in an Austrian province who retraced his steps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doubled back' looks like a return journey; it tells you to double the back letter. Y is one of the algebraic unknowns, alongside X and Z.
explanation.definitionFit: A folklore creature: Scandinavian tales picture these as ugly, often dwarfish beings.

clue.text: Mastery of European, cheeky one, in kinky sex

indicators.note: one thing placed in another sits inside it
something kinked is bent out of shape, so its letters are twisted into a new order

parts.note: E = European
joined with E, anagram fodder that splits around the middle
pert = cheeky, saucy
I = one, the Roman numeral

explanation.surface: A European's skill in cheeky, unconventional lovemaking.
explanation.walkthrough: The commas make 'cheeky one' look like a description of the European, but the European's letter belongs with the anagram, not with the insert.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: great skill or knowledge in a field is mastery of it.

clue.text: Old old Scotsman's outside loop

indicators.note: one word standing outside another wraps round it

parts.note: the Picts were an ancient people of Scotland
O = old

explanation.surface: An elderly Scot circles around a roundabout.
explanation.walkthrough: The Picts were the ancient inhabitants of northern Scotland, hence an 'old Scotsman'.
explanation.definitionFit: A needlework term: the tiny ornamental loops of thread along an edge of lace or ribbon.

clue.text: Provided funding for outstanding result?

parts.note: an end is an outcome, a result
an outstanding debt is still owed

explanation.surface: Someone financed a project because of its excellent outcome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outstanding result' reads as praise; 'outstanding' means unpaid, and the two pieces come in reverse order from the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to give an institution a lasting income is to fund it.

clue.text: Overturn limit with audible expressions of regret

parts.note: a cap is an upper limit

indicators.note: audible means heard, so the word is taken by its sound, not its spelling

parts.note: sighs express regret; spoken, they sound like SIZE

explanation.surface: Reversing a spending ceiling amid loud sighs of disappointment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Overturn' looks legal, like overturning a verdict, but it is a boat turning over.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the nautical sense: a boat that tips upside down has overturned.

clue.text: Watch door in study being smashed

indicators.note: one thing placed in another sits inside it
something smashed is broken apart, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder, rearranged so it splits after its first letter
a door is an entry

explanation.surface: Guarding the entrance to a room that has been broken into.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Study' reads as a room whose door is being smashed; it is the anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym: a guard's spell on duty is a watch, as a ship's crew keeps watches.

clue.text: Not so much to consecrate in bishop's absence

indicators.note: 'in the absence of' frames the removal: the word is taken as it would be without that letter
something absent is missing, so its letter is dropped

parts.note: to bless is to consecrate
B, bishop in chess notation, is removed

explanation.surface: A reduced ceremony because the bishop failed to turn up.
explanation.walkthrough: B stands for bishop, as in chess notation; the bishop fits the church scene, which is why he goes unnoticed.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the comparative of 'little' means a smaller amount, not so much.
